Chest, Abdomen, and Pelvis on the Image: Heart, Lungs, Liver, GI and Urinary Tracts

Unit 1: Anatomy, Positioning, and Medical Language. Lesson 2 of 60 in CRES Academy.

Three quarters of the volume a general radiographic room produces is chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Knowing what those images are meant to show tells you when a complaint is a fault and when it is a technique choice.

The heart and the chest image

The heart is a four-chamber pump: the right side sends blood to the lungs, the left side sends it to the body. Blood leaves the right side through the pulmonary artery to the lungs and returns through the pulmonary vein to the left side, which pushes it out through arteries, then arterioles, then capillaries, and back through venules and veins; the heart with those vessels is the cardiovascular system, the circulatory system the outline names. On a chest image the heart appears as a silhouette against air-filled lung, and its width compared with the chest is one of the first things read, so geometry matters: a posteroanterior projection at the long distance keeps the heart close to the detector and near its true size, while an anteroposterior portable at a short distance magnifies it. A radiologist complaining that hearts look large on one room is making a distance and projection comment, which is yours to check.

Lungs, airway, diaphragm, and pleura

Air enters through the trachea, divides into the bronchi, and ends in the alveoli where gas is exchanged. The diaphragm is the muscle below the lungs that drives breathing, and the pleura is the double membrane around each lung. Images are taken on full inspiration because the lungs are then largest and the diaphragm lowest; an expiration image looks crowded and underexposed and is a repeat. Pathologies the chest is ordered for, at recognition level, are pneumonia (fluid and consolidation), pneumothorax (air outside the lung), pleural effusion (fluid in the space), and heart enlargement.

Abdomen: liver, gallbladder, and the gastrointestinal tract

The gastrointestinal tract runs mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum), large intestine or colon, rectum, and anus. The liver sits high on the right and makes bile, the gallbladder stores it, and the pancreas adds digestive enzymes. Abdominal images are ordered for obstruction, free air after a perforation, stones, and foreign bodies.

Urinary system

Two kidneys filter blood, the ureters carry urine down, the bladder stores it, and the urethra carries it out. Stones and obstruction are the common reasons for imaging.

Contrast by system

Air (negative)        Bowel gas and double-contrast studies; absorbs little, so it reads dark
Barium sulfate        Swallowed or given as an enema for the gastrointestinal tract; not injected
Iodinated contrast    Vessels, the urinary tract, and cross-sectional work; given by vein or catheter
Sensitivity           Always checked before administration, so reaction supplies stay in the room

What each exam demands of the equipment

  • Chest: a high kilovoltage technique, above 100 kVp, for latitude through lung and mediastinum, at the long source-to-image distance, erect, on inspiration.
  • Abdomen: a grid, because a thick trunk scatters heavily, and the shortest practical time, because bowel moves.
  • Pelvis: careful collimation and shielding of what is not being imaged, because the gonads are in or near the field.
Exam tip: the heart is the pump, the diaphragm drives breathing, and chest images are taken on inspiration. Barium goes in the gastrointestinal tract, iodinated contrast goes into vessels and the urinary tract. Chest means high kilovoltage and a long distance; abdomen means a grid.
Remember
The heart pumps right side to lungs and left side to body and shows as a silhouette whose size depends on projection and distance; lungs, trachea, diaphragm, and pleura are imaged erect on inspiration; the gastrointestinal tract runs mouth to anus with liver, gallbladder, and pancreas alongside; kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra make the urinary tract; barium images the gut, iodinated contrast the vessels and urinary tract, and chest work needs high kilovoltage while abdomen needs a grid.
Deeper explanation

Chest, Abdomen, and Pelvis on the Image: Heart, Lungs, Liver, GI and Urinary Tracts, explained slowly

Reading a chest image the way the room has to produce it

A chest radiograph is asked to show four things at once: aerated lung, the heart's outline, the mediastinum behind it, and the bones around it. Those tissues differ enormously in how much they absorb, so the exam is a latitude problem. That is the whole reason chest work uses a high kilovoltage technique, above 100 kVp: high kilovoltage penetrates the dense mediastinum without burning out the lungs, at the price of lower contrast, which a grid partly buys back.

Geometry is why hearts look different room to room

Setup                       Heart on the image        What you check when it is questioned
PA, erect, 180 cm           closest to true size      distance indicator, detent, erect detector height
AP, portable, short         magnified, less sharp     distance scale on the column, OID, technique chart
Expiration instead of       crowded lung, raised      nothing on the machine; it is a breathing instruction
inspiration                 diaphragm

The magnification factor is the source-to-image distance divided by the source-to-object distance, which is about 1.1 at 100 cm and about 1.05 at 180 cm. So the long distance is not a tradition, it is how the heart's measured width stays meaningful. A radiologist who says one room makes hearts look big is telling you the distance or the projection in that room has changed.

Respiratory anatomy, in the order air travels

Trachea, then the main bronchi, then smaller branches, then alveoli where oxygen and carbon dioxide trade places. The diaphragm below the lungs is the muscle that does the work of breathing, and the pleura is the double membrane wrapping each lung with a thin space between the layers. Imaging is done on full inspiration because that is when the lungs are largest, the diaphragm lowest, and the most lung visible.

  • Pneumonia fills air spaces with fluid, so lung that should be dark turns gray.
  • Pneumothorax is air in the pleural space, which collapses lung and needs an erect or decubitus image to find the edge.
  • Pleural effusion is fluid in that space, which settles, so a horizontal beam shows its level.
  • An enlarged heart is read from its width against the chest, which is why geometry comes first.

The abdomen and pelvis

The GI tract runs mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine as duodenum, jejunum, and ileum, then the colon, rectum, and anus, with the liver high on the right making bile, the gallbladder storing it, and the pancreas adding enzymes. The urinary system is two kidneys filtering blood, two ureters carrying urine down, the bladder holding it, and the urethra passing it out. Abdominal images are ordered for obstruction, perforation and free air, stones, and swallowed objects; urinary studies for stones and obstruction.

Contrast, by what it does to the beam

Agent               Given how                        Why
Air                 swallowed, or with barium        absorbs little, so it reads dark and outlines walls
Barium sulfate      swallowed or as an enema         dense, not absorbed by the body, stays in the tract
Iodinated contrast  by vein, artery, or catheter     dense and carried in blood, so vessels and the
                                                     urinary system fill and can be followed

Sensitivity to a contrast agent is checked before it is given, which is why reaction supplies and trained staff are part of a contrast room and why your service work there includes the injector, its interlocks, and the room's suction and oxygen outlets.

What each region demands of the equipment

  • Chest: high kilovoltage above 100 kVp, the long distance, erect, on inspiration, short exposure time.
  • Abdomen: a grid, because a thick trunk scatters heavily, and the shortest practical time, because bowel moves.
  • Pelvis: accurate collimation and shielding of what is not imaged, because the gonads are in or beside the field; so the collimator lamp and light field accuracy are a dose item here, not a convenience.

What to memorize

  • Heart right side to lungs, left side to body; chest images erect, PA, long distance, on inspiration.
  • Trachea, bronchi, alveoli, diaphragm, pleura; pneumonia, pneumothorax, effusion.
  • The tract in order with liver, gallbladder, and pancreas; kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra.
  • Air and barium for the tract, iodinated contrast for vessels and the urinary system, sensitivity checked first.
